Utah Governor Spencer Cox confirmed that bullet casings from Tyler Robinson’s weapon, used in the killing of Charlie Kirk, were inscribed with phrases drawn from internet culture.⁠ ⁠ One read “Notices bulges OwO, what’s this?”—a meme phrase from furry and anime role-play communities that spread online as parody copypasta. Another said “Hey fascist! Catch!”—a slogan echoing antifascist activist language. A third inscription carried the lyrics “Oh bella ciao, bella ciao, bella ciao ciao ciao,” from the Italian partisan folk song Bella Ciao, now used globally as a protest anthem. The final casing read “If you read this you are gay LMAO,” a trolling meme format familiar across social media and gaming forums.⁠ ⁠ On Thursday, The Wall Street Journal had previously reported, citing an internal law enforcement bulletin, that the ammunition was “engraved with expressions of transgender and antifascist ideology.”⁠ ⁠ While that claim has not been fully retracted, the paper has since updated its coverage, noting the bulletin “may not accurately reflect the messages on the ammunition” and that “some officials later Thursday cautioned against reaching conclusions based on the internal report.”⁠

Are you the type to admire others ? I feel as though while that can be quite healthy to a degree there’s also a lot of nuance in that concept. While most would dream of suffering from success some people actually get to suffer from it, unwanted attention all around and being treated differently no matter where you go how you go and why you go can be quite suffocating. It’s also quite easy to objectify people we admire, what we admire them for easily ends up becoming an obsession that is all we end up seeing when looking at them, like some kind of shield that would let our vision bounce off before getting to observe anything further. It has to be quite exhausting, being loved an hated for the exact same reasons again and again yet people don’t even take the time to stop and try to look at who you truly are. Your worth is nothing but that one societal value that everyone wants yet sometimes you didn’t even ask for it, hell you wish you didn’t even have it at times. To you all I say, treat those who have what you don’t which you deeply desire the same way. Maybe tell them about how incredible that is but don’t start with that as they have probably heard it far too often and are starting to think as though they are nothing but the metaphor of that value. Treat those stuck in a routine that is forced upon them differently, tell them how you value another aspect of them so much no one had never even bothered taking a glance at before. Don’t objectify them because they possess something you don’t that you deeply desire, rather act even more freely with such people, they will most definitely enjoy your consideration and care.

Actor and comedian Jerry Seinfeld denounced the “Free Palestine” movement as antisemitic in a surprise appearance at a Duke event Tuesday, likening it to rhetoric from the Ku Klux Klan during his introduction of a former Israeli hostage. “Free Palestine is, to me, just — you’re free to say you don’t like Jews. Just say you don’t like Jews,” Seinfeld said. “By saying Free Palestine, you’re not admitting what you really think,” he continued. “So it’s actually — compared to the Ku Klux Klan, I’m actually thinking the climate is actually a little better here because they can come right out and say, ‘We don’t like Blacks, we don’t like Jews.’ Okay that’s honest.” Seinfeld made the comments at an event with Omer Shem Tov, a former Israeli hostage who was abducted by Hamas at the Oct. 7, 2023, Nova music festival and held captive for 505 days. The event was sponsored primarily by Chabad at Duke, as well as the Provost’s Initiative on the Middle East, University centers and Jewish student groups. Seinfeld’s remarks came as part of a brief introduction to Shem Tov and the event’s moderator, N.C. State Sen. Sophia Chitlik, D-Durham. His appearance at the event, which was open only to Duke students, faculty and staff, was not publicized beforehand. The event was organized by student groups alongside the University, but Duke administrators dodged responsibility for Seinfeld’s presence.
